title: Seven Rules and Their Exceptions
principle: Nothing is alive because of one sign.

t: There is a list of seven things living things do. Every single one has something that breaks it.
Textbooks give seven signs of life. Each one has a well-known exception, and the exceptions are more interesting than the list.
sub: A definition that fails at the edges is not necessarily a bad definition. But it is worth knowing where it fails.

stages.label: Go through the seven
captions: Moves — but a tree stays put its whole life.
Breathes — but some bacteria are poisoned by oxygen.
Senses things — but a sponge has no nerves at all.
Grows — but a crystal grows too, and is not alive.
Gets rid of waste — so does a car engine.
Has young — but a mule has none, and a worker bee never will.
Eats — but a plant makes its own out of light.
t: Slide through the seven signs. Each one has something that breaks it.
Each sign, with its standard counter-example. Watch for the ones where the exception is a living thing failing the test.
after: Not one of the seven works on its own.
No single criterion is necessary and sufficient. Note the two kinds of failure: things that are alive and fail a test, and things that pass a test and are not alive.

question: If every rule has an exception, is the list useless?
Given that each criterion admits counter-examples, what is the list good for?
options: No — you need most of them at once, not any one
Yes, it should be thrown away
Yes, unless you can find a rule with no exceptions
stages.outcome: No — you need most of them at once, not any one
note: Commit. The same structure appears in medical diagnosis, where no single symptom is decisive either.

t: Nothing is alive because of one sign. It is alive because of most of them together.
Life is recognised by a cluster of properties, not by any single test. The list works collectively even though every item fails alone.
This is a cluster concept: membership is conferred by satisfying enough of a set of criteria, none of which is individually necessary.

Wittgenstein's family-resemblance account fits this exactly — the members of a category can share no single common feature and still form a real category. Biology is full of these, and treating them as if they had crisp definitions produces most of the confusion around viruses.
sub: A tree does not move and a mule has no babies. Both are clearly alive.
Failing one criterion is not disqualifying, which is why the list survives its own exceptions.
The interesting entries are the ones failing many at once — a virus outside a cell does none of the seven.
Cluster concepts do not have sharp boundaries and do not need them. The demand for a crisp definition is where the trouble starts, not the lack of one.

q: A tree cannot walk. Is it alive?
A tree does not move from its position. Does that count against it being alive?
How should a single failed criterion be weighed?
options: Yes — it does nearly all the others
why: Missing one sign does not matter much. A tree grows, uses energy, senses light, gets rid of waste and makes seeds — that is plenty.
One failure carries almost no weight in a cluster concept. A tree satisfies six of seven comfortably, and moving turns out to be the least important of them.

Weight it as evidence rather than as a gate. This is why 'is a virus alive?' has no clean answer and does not need one — the useful question is which properties it has and which it lacks, and that question does have an answer.

t: Doctors have to decide when a person has died, and that turns out to be just as hard.

The legal and medical definition of death has been rewritten more than once as technology changed what could be maintained. Brain-death criteria exist because the older tests — heartbeat, breathing — stopped tracking what they were meant to track once machines could supply both. The boundary problem is not academic.
